Google Will Place Solar-Powered AI Data Centers in Space Using the Blue Origin New Glenn Rocket
12 photos
Photo: Blue Origin
When Elon Musk decided it would be a good idea to place Internet satellites in orbit, a lot of people probably asked themselves how come they didn't think about this first. It was a brilliant thought that opened up worlds of possibilities, as Internet from space can reach any place on the planet, regardless of what's happening on the ground. And now the world seems ready for the next step.
While a number of companies (and even countries) are now following in SpaceX's footsteps and are building their own Internet satellite constellations, Google is thinking about something different. That would be the creation of AI data centers in orbit, capable of harnessing the power of the Sun to work - as a side note, SpaceX is working on something similar, they call it Starmind .
Google seems to be a bit ahead of Elon Musk's company in this respect, as it has already decided when the first AI satellite will be placed in orbit, and who will transport it there. That would be 2029, and Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket, respectively.
Jeff Bezos' space company is the one that announced this week that Google will deploy to orbit, before the end of the decade, the first elements of its AI constellation, which is for now known as Project Suncatcher. The New Glenn will carry it into sun-synchronous orbit in the first quarter of 2029.
It's unclear how many of these satellites will fly on this first mission, but we do know that each of them will have the computing capacity of a data center rack. They will have the ability to harness the solar power that's abundant, continuous, and free in space, and they'll be equipped with AI chips Google likes to call Tensor Processing Units (TPUs).
There is a long road to travel before getting there, though. Google has been working on the idea for years, and only recently transformed it into something real by launching a first prototype using SpaceX's Transporter-18 mission in October 2026.
The hardware is about the size of a refrigerator, and it is equipped with four TPUs. Its purpose is to allow the technology giant to test spaceflight stress, radiation, and the thermal limits of the hardware. The mission is scheduled to last about a year and includes running a series of AI workloads like the DeepMind Gemma open model.
Come next year, Google plans to launch an additional two satellites (it's unclear who will handle this particular launch), destined to test high-speed laser communications between orbiting spacecraft – something that's crucial to making the AI data center network worthwhile.
If everything checks out, the company will move to start building the orbital network itself, probably sometime early next decade. We'll keep an eye on this story and report back once we know more.
